lens: What problem is Machiavelli solving here?

difficulty.why: Short chapters and plain prose, but packed with Italian history you are not expected to know.

parts.title: Before the book
parts.question: Why should Lorenzo de' Medici listen to an exiled official?

parts.title: I · Kinds of states and how to win them
parts.question: What kinds of power are there, and how is each won and kept?
parts.arc: From the easy case, an inherited state, to the hard ones: power won by ability, by luck, by crime or by the people.

groups.title: What there is to rule
groups.question: Which states are easy to keep, and why?

groups.title: Holding what you take
groups.question: How do you keep a territory you have just conquered?

groups.title: Rising to power
groups.question: Ability, luck, crime or the people: which way up lasts?

groups.title: Special cases
groups.question: How strong are you, and why is the Church different?

parts.title: II · Armies
parts.question: Whose soldiers can a ruler trust?
parts.arc: Hired armies fail, borrowed ones are worse, so a prince must have his own and study war.

groups.title: Hired and borrowed armies
groups.question: Why can't you buy or borrow your safety?

groups.title: The prince as soldier
groups.question: What should a ruler spend his time learning?

parts.title: III · How a prince should behave
parts.question: Should a ruler be good, or only seem good?
parts.arc: The book's famous turn: from imagined virtue to what actually keeps a ruler in power.

groups.title: Being good and seeming good
groups.question: Which virtues can a ruler afford?

groups.title: Staying safe and respected
groups.question: What brings rulers down, and what earns esteem?

groups.title: The people around you
groups.question: Whose advice should a ruler trust?

parts.title: IV · Italy and fortune
parts.question: Is Italy's ruin bad luck, or can it be undone?
parts.arc: Blame idleness, not fortune; fortune can be resisted; then a call to free Italy.

groups.title: Luck and blame
groups.question: How much is in our hands?

routes.title: The essentials
routes.line: Nine chapters, starting at the book's turning point: chapter 15.

stops.problem: How does an official out of favour get a ruler to listen?
stops.meet: Machiavelli offers Lorenzo de' Medici his one valuable possession: what he knows of the deeds of great men.
stops.watch: Read it as a job application. He wrote in exile, after the Medici returned to Florence in 1512.
stops.summary: Machiavelli presents the book to Lorenzo de' Medici as a gift of practical knowledge drawn from long experience and reading, written plainly and without ornament. He asks Lorenzo to see the hardships of its author.

stops.problem: What kinds of state are there?
stops.meet: The book's map: principalities are inherited or new, and new ones are won by your own arms or others', by fortune or by ability.
stops.watch: This two-line scheme organises everything up to chapter 11.
stops.summary: States are republics or principalities; this book is about principalities. They are hereditary or new, and new ones are acquired by one's own arms or those of others, through fortune or through ability (virtù).

stops.problem: Why are inherited states easy to keep?
stops.meet: Habit does the work: an ordinary prince keeps such a state unless an extraordinary force removes him.
stops.watch: A quick contrast that sets up the hard case of new princes.
stops.summary: Inherited states are easy to hold because people are used to the ruling family. A prince of average ability keeps them by not disturbing old customs, and wins them back even if he loses them.

stops.problem: How do you hold a territory you have just added to your state?
stops.meet: Go and live there or plant colonies; weaken strong neighbours and protect weak ones; Louis XII's six mistakes in Italy.
stops.watch: Long and thick with French and Italian history. Skim the history, keep the rules.
stops.summary: New additions to a state rebel because new subjects expected better and were disappointed. The remedies: live in the territory, plant colonies, make yourself head of the weaker neighbours and crush the strong. Louis XII lost Milan by breaking all these rules.

stops.problem: Why are some conquests easy to keep and others not?
stops.meet: Turkey, ruled by one master with servants, against France, ruled with powerful barons.
stops.watch: A structural argument: a centralised state is hard to take but easy to hold.
stops.summary: A state run by one ruler and his servants is hard to conquer but easy to hold once taken, as Persia was for Alexander. A state of a prince and barons is easy to enter but hard to keep, because the barons remain.

stops.problem: What do you do with a city used to governing itself?
stops.meet: Three options: ruin it, live there, or let it keep its laws under a few friendly rulers.
stops.watch: His harshest advice sits in a short chapter. When he says ruin, he means it.
stops.summary: A free city can be held by destroying it, by living in it, or by letting it keep its laws under an oligarchy friendly to you. The memory of liberty never sleeps, so destruction is the surest way.

stops.problem: What made founders like Moses, Cyrus and Romulus succeed?
stops.meet: Opportunity met by ability; new institutions are the hardest thing to introduce; armed prophets win and unarmed ones fall.
stops.watch: Virtù and fortuna, the book's two key words, are set out here.
stops.summary: Great founders owed fortune only the opportunity; their ability did the rest. Introducing a new order is hard because the old order's beneficiaries resist and its friends are lukewarm, so a founder must be able to use force: armed prophets win, unarmed ones like Savonarola fail.

stops.problem: Can someone who rises by luck stay on top?
stops.meet: Cesare Borgia's methods, the execution of Remirro de Orco at Cesena, and his fall when his father died.
stops.watch: Machiavelli admires Borgia, yet the story ends in failure. Ask why.
stops.summary: Those who rise by others' arms or by luck rise easily and struggle to stay. Cesare Borgia, made by his father the Pope, built his own power skilfully: he won over Romagna through Remirro de Orco's harsh rule, then had him executed. His only error was letting Julius II become Pope.

inside.question: Why is power won by luck so fragile?
inside.line: The rule: what rises fast falls fast, unless the prince lays foundations afterwards.

inside.question: Two ways up: Sforza and Borgia
inside.line: Sforza rose by his own ability; Borgia by his father the Pope.

inside.question: How did Borgia build power of his own?
inside.line: Weakening the Orsini and Colonna, the trap at Sinigalia, Romagna and Remirro de Orco, planning for the next Pope.

inside.question: What brought him down?
inside.line: His father died while he lay ill himself.

inside.question: Was he to blame?
inside.line: Machiavelli would hold him up as a model, with one mistake: Julius II.

stops.problem: Can crime win a state and keep it?
stops.meet: Agathocles and Oliverotto; cruelty 'well used': all at once, then turned to the subjects' benefit.
stops.watch: He refuses to call Agathocles' crimes virtù, a rare moral line in the book.
stops.summary: Agathocles and Oliverotto seized power by murder. Machiavelli says such methods can win power but not glory. Cruelty is well used when done all at once and for security, then turned to the subjects' good; badly used when it grows over time.

stops.problem: Should a new prince lean on the nobles or on the people?
stops.meet: The people only want not to be oppressed; no prince is safe against a hostile people.
stops.watch: The book's most 'popular' chapter, in tension with much of the rest.
stops.summary: A prince raised by the nobles struggles, because they see themselves as his equals; one raised by the people stands more securely. The people's aim is more honest than the nobles': not to be oppressed. A prince must keep the people friendly, above all in adversity.

stops.problem: How can you tell whether a state can stand alone?
stops.meet: Can you raise an army for open battle, or must you hide behind walls? The German cities.
stops.watch: Short and practical.
stops.summary: A strong state can field an army against any attacker. Otherwise a prince should fortify his city, stock it for a siege and keep his people's spirits up, as the German cities do.

stops.problem: Why are states of the Church held without effort?
stops.meet: They rest on ancient religious institutions; how Alexander VI and Julius II made the papacy a power.
stops.watch: Watch his ironic tone towards the Church.
stops.summary: Ecclesiastical states are acquired by ability or fortune but held by old religious institutions, which keep rulers in place however they behave. The Church's temporal power grew late, mainly under Alexander VI and Julius II.

stops.problem: Why do hired armies fail?
stops.meet: Mercenaries are disunited, ambitious and faithless; Italy's ruin rests on them.
stops.watch: Here is his core claim: there are no good laws without good arms.
stops.summary: The foundations of every state are good laws and good arms, and good arms come first. Mercenaries are useless and dangerous: brave among friends, cowardly before enemies. Italy's ruin comes from relying on them for years.

stops.problem: Is borrowing another state's army any better?
stops.meet: Worse: win and you are their prisoner. David refusing Saul's armour.
stops.watch: It builds towards one rule: rely on your own arms.
stops.summary: Auxiliary troops lent by a stronger power are even more dangerous than mercenaries, because they are united and loyal to someone else. A wise prince relies on his own soldiers; victory with others' arms is not true victory.

stops.problem: What should a prince study?
stops.meet: War, and only war: hunting to learn ground, history to imitate great men.
stops.watch: Short and blunt.
stops.summary: A prince's one proper profession is war. In peace he should train his body and mind: hunt to learn terrain and read history to imitate great commanders.

stops.problem: Should a ruler be good?
stops.meet: His famous turn to 'the effectual truth of the thing' over imagined republics: a prince must learn how not to be good.
stops.watch: The book's pivot. If you read one chapter, read this.
stops.summary: Many have written of ideal states that never existed. Machiavelli writes about how people actually live. Since a ruler surrounded by bad men will be ruined by being good in every way, he must learn how not to be good and use that as necessity requires.

stops.problem: Is generosity a virtue in a ruler?
stops.meet: Showy generosity ruins you through taxes; better a name for being mean.
stops.watch: He separates spending your own money from spending other people's.
stops.summary: Generosity practised to be seen forces a prince to tax his people and become hated. Better to accept a reputation for meanness, which harms few, than lose everything chasing a reputation for generosity, except with plunder taken from others.

stops.problem: Is it better to be loved or feared?
stops.meet: Feared, if you can't be both, but never hated: leave people's property and women alone. Hannibal against Scipio.
stops.watch: Usually quoted without its condition: never be hated.
stops.summary: A prince should want to be thought merciful but must not misuse mercy. Since it is hard to be both loved and feared, it is safer to be feared, because love depends on others and fear on yourself, provided you avoid being hated, which means leaving subjects' property and women alone.

stops.problem: Must a prince keep his promises?
stops.meet: The fox and the lion: seem merciful, faithful, humane and religious, and be able to be otherwise.
stops.watch: The most notorious chapter. Note that he is talking about appearances.
stops.summary: There are two ways to fight, by law and by force, and a prince must know both: the fox to spot traps and the lion to frighten wolves. He need not keep faith when it works against him, but must appear to have every virtue, because people judge by appearances and results.

stops.problem: What actually brings rulers down?
stops.meet: Contempt and hatred, conspiracies, and a long survey of Roman emperors from Marcus Aurelius to Maximinus.
stops.watch: The longest chapter. The emperor survey can be skimmed.
stops.summary: A prince falls through hatred and contempt. He is hated for seizing property and women, despised for being fickle or weak. A ruler loved by his people need not fear conspiracies. The Roman emperors show the point, squeezed between the people and the army.

stops.problem: Do fortresses keep you safe?
stops.meet: Arm your subjects rather than disarm them; the best fortress is not being hated.
stops.watch: Practical dilemmas with mixed answers.
stops.summary: New princes do well to arm their subjects, and those who disarm them breed distrust. Fortresses help a prince who fears his people more than foreigners, and harm one who fears foreigners more. The best fortress is not to be hated.

stops.problem: How does a prince win esteem?
stops.meet: Great undertakings like Ferdinand of Aragon's, taking sides rather than staying neutral, and rewarding citizens.
stops.watch: The argument against neutrality is still applied today.
stops.summary: Nothing builds esteem like great undertakings and rare examples, as Ferdinand of Aragon showed. A prince should be a true friend or a true enemy; neutrality leaves him prey to the winner. He should honour talent and encourage trade and the arts.

stops.problem: How do you judge a ruler?
stops.meet: By the people around him: the three kinds of minds.
stops.watch: A short chapter. Machiavelli was himself a secretary.
stops.summary: The first judgement of a ruler's mind comes from the men he keeps around him. A good minister thinks of the prince, never of himself, and the prince keeps him loyal with honours and wealth.

stops.problem: How do you get honest advice?
stops.meet: Let a few chosen wise men speak freely, but only when asked.
stops.watch: Good advice, he says, depends on the prince's own good sense.
stops.summary: Courts are full of flatterers. A prince should choose a few wise advisers, let them speak the truth when he asks, then decide himself and hold to it. Good counsel comes from the prince's prudence, not the reverse.

stops.problem: Why did Italy's rulers lose their states?
stops.meet: Not bad luck, but their own idleness and lack of arms.
stops.watch: It sets up the last two chapters.
stops.summary: The princes of Italy who lost their states should blame their own idleness, not fortune. They trusted to calm weather, had no armies of their own, and fled instead of defending themselves.

stops.problem: How much of life does fortune control?
stops.meet: About half: fortune is a river you can bank against, and, in his famous image, a woman to be mastered.
stops.watch: Philosophically the richest chapter. The gendered image dates it.
stops.summary: Fortune governs half of our actions and leaves the other half to us. Like a flooding river it can be checked by dykes built in calm times. Since times change and people do not, success depends on fitting your nature to the times, and it is better to be bold than cautious.

stops.problem: Who will free Italy from foreign armies?
stops.meet: A rousing call to the Medici, ending with lines from Petrarch.
stops.watch: The tone changes completely: rhetoric, not analysis.
stops.summary: Italy is ready for a redeemer, and the Medici house, favoured by fortune and the Church, could lead with its own new army. Machiavelli ends with Petrarch's call that ancient Italian valour is not yet dead.

question: How does a new ruler win power, and keep it, in a world that does not reward goodness?
